section.title: Additional topics: contraction and fixed-point iteration

introduction.p: A fixed-point equation can identify a possible limit, but the examples in showed that this is not enough to prove convergence. A contraction supplies the missing control. This optional section uses the Cauchy criterion to prove existence, uniqueness, and usable error estimates.

subsection.title: Distance, completeness, and contraction
subsection.p: On a closed interval D=[a,b], measure distance by d(x,y)=|x-y|. A map T:D\to D is a contraction if there is a constant q, with 0\le q<1, such that

The requirement T(D)\subseteq D keeps every iterate inside the set where the estimate holds. By the Mean Value Theorem, a differentiable map on the interval is a contraction if |T'(x)|\le q<1 throughout it.

The same argument works for other kinds of objects. A metric space is a set D equipped with a distance d that is nonnegative, is zero exactly when its inputs are equal, satisfies d(x,y)=d(y,x), and obeys the triangle inequality d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z). A sequence is Cauchy when d(x_m,x_n) becomes arbitrarily small for all sufficiently large m,n. The space is complete if every Cauchy sequence converges to an element of D. Closed real intervals are complete by and the preservation of inequalities under limits.

subsection.title: The contraction theorem and its error estimates

statement.p: Let D be a nonempty complete metric space and let T:D\to D be a contraction with constant q<1. There is exactly one fixed point x_*\in D. For every starting point x_0\in D, the iteration x_{n+1}=T(x_n) converges to x_*. For n\ge1,

proof.p: Repeated contraction gives d(x_{k+1},x_k)\le q^k d(x_1,x_0). For m>n, the triangle inequality and the finite geometric sum give

Thus the iterates are Cauchy and have a limit x_*\in D. The contraction inequality implies continuity of T, so taking the limit in x_{n+1}=T(x_n) gives x_*=T(x_*). Two fixed points would satisfy d(x_*,y_*)\le qd(x_*,y_*), forcing their distance to be zero.
Letting m\to\infty in the finite-tail bound proves the first estimate. Starting the same geometric bound at the most recent step proves the second. For any x\in D,
Rearranging proves the residual estimate, including the third bound. If q=0, the map is constant and one step already reaches its fixed point.

subsection.p: The first bound is an a priori estimate: it can predict an iteration count from the initial step. The second is an a posteriori estimate: it uses the step just computed. In exact arithmetic, stop with an error at most \varepsilon when q|x_n-x_{n-1}|/(1-q)\le\varepsilon. A small step alone is not the bound; the factor q/(1-q) matters, especially when q is near one.

This follows by iterating e_{n+1}\le qe_n+\delta. It explains the error floor caused by inaccurate function evaluations or rounding. A certified residual bound must include those evaluation errors.

example.title: Solving x=\cos x
example.p: The map T(x)=\cos x sends [0,1] into itself. On that interval, |T'(x)|=\sin x\le\sin1<0.85, so take q=0.85. Starting at x_0=1 gives x_1\approx0.540302, x_2\approx0.857553, and eventually x_*\approx0.739085. The theorem proves convergence for every start in the interval, even though the iterates need not be monotone. The residual estimate bounds the distance to the root by |x-\cos x|/0.15.

warning.title: Why the set and the constant matter
warning.p: The contraction T(x)=x/2 on the open interval (0,1) has no fixed point there: its iterates tend to zero outside the set. Completeness prevents this escape. On [0,1], the map T(x)=1-x has a fixed point but contraction constant only 1; most iterates oscillate. Neither hypothesis can simply be discarded.

exercise.title: Prove convergence and choose a stopping rule

statement.p: For T(x)=(x+2)/3 on [0,2], prove the self-map and contraction properties, identify the fixed point, and find an a priori iteration count guaranteeing error at most 10^{-6} when x_0=0. Express an a posteriori stopping test.

hint.p: Use q=1/3, x_*=1, and |x_1-x_0|=2/3. The first bound is 3^{-n}, so n=13 suffices. Stop when |x_n-x_{n-1}|/2\le10^{-6}.
